source.title: Pretrained Transformers Do not Always Improve Robustness
source.authors: Swaroop Mishra; Bhavdeep Singh Sachdeva; Chitta Baral

record.tranche_reason: Tests robustness to randomly flipped training labels in NLP sentiment classification, an extension beyond the original image-labeling setting; reports validation accuracy across corruption levels.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-accuracy outcomes for label-flipping levels. It does not report zero training error on fully random labels or training time to convergence. The cited image-model random-label result is prior work, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4's generalization component in sentiment classification by measuring validation accuracy across training-label corruption levels. It also reports training–validation gaps, but does not demonstrate perfect training fit throughout the sweep.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: in these two sentiment datasets, pretrained Transformers can be less robust to label flipping than LSTMs and simpler models under MRAP, despite higher validation accuracy. RoBERTa-based adversarial filtering does not reliably distinguish poisoned from unpoisoned examples.
record.recipe_differences: NLP sentiment classification with label flipping at 0%, 30%, 50%, 70% and 90%; models include bag-of-words, embedding-based networks and pretrained Transformers. The study lightly tunes learning rate and number of epochs to maximize validation performance.
record.method_sensitivity: Label-flipping percentage and dataset; the paper reports variation across models and datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Model rankings by NMRAP differ from rankings by clean validation accuracy; LSTMs and simpler models can outperform pretrained Transformers on this robustness metric.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher clean accuracy and greater pretraining do not necessarily imply greater robustness to training-label flipping.

fits_no_version.finding: AFPLite predictability scores do not reliably separate flipped-label examples from unflipped examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial filtering using RoBERTa embeddings does not reliably detect label poisoning in these experiments.

record.code_released: not stated; code is attached in supplementary material and will be open sourced upon acceptance
record.problems: Only two datasets are used. The study reports validation accuracy and training-validation gaps, but does not establish perfect training fit across corruption levels; some findings are presented in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No rows extracted because the reported values are validation accuracy under label flipping, while V4 requires results showing both perfect training fit and validation/test degradation. Individual model values appear in Table 3 and Table 4; training-validation differences appear in Table 5 and Figure 4.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error on completely random labels under unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training time and convergence slowdown relative to true labels.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit throughout corruption levels; the fully corrupted endpoint; memorization of noise alongside remaining signal. Learning rate and epoch count are tuned for validation performance.
Effects of removing or adding weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation.
The temporal order of learning shared patterns and memorizing noisy labels.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's limits_scope rationale based solely on unestablished perfect training fit; an untested component is not adverse evidence. The relevant numerical results and training–validation gaps are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as undeclared missing results. Table 3 reports maximum validation accuracies, not training accuracies. Binary flipping at 90% is not equivalent to independent random labeling: it preserves substantial information under label inversion.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report whether training error reaches zero or near zero on a completely random labeling, or test error at chance in that setting.
Training time and convergence slowdown are not reported.
Shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.

Validation accuracy is reported across label-flipping levels, but the study does not establish that training error remains perfect at each level. Individual model-level values across the full sweep are not extracted here.
The study does not test weight decay, dropout or data augmentation as causes of fitting or generalization.
The study does not measure the order in which real patterns and noisy labels are learned.

relationships.condition: Validation degradation from 0% through 30% to 50% label flipping
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict; no rows were extracted. Table 3 shows declining maximum validation accuracy for all ten models, reaching 49.08–51.55% at 50% flipping. This supports the degradation component only.
relationships.display_finding: Maximum validation accuracy declined for all ten models, reaching 49.08–51.55% at 50% label flipping.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Validation degradation from 0% through 30% to 50% label flipping
source_check.reason: Text-based: Table 3 shows declining maximum validation accuracy for all ten models across these levels, reaching 49.08–51.55% at 50% flipping. Supports the tested degradation component; perfect training fit remains untested.

relationships.condition: Binary label flipping above 50%, with the paper's reversed procedure and label interpretation
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict; no rows were extracted. Section 3(q3) and Table 3 show recovery rather than steady degradation: BERT-large rises from 50.86% at 50% flipping to 89.35% at 70% and 92.44% at 90%. The authors attribute recovery to flipped label interpretation, so this protocol does not represent progressively less informative random labels.
relationships.display_finding: With reversed label interpretation, accuracy rose from 50.86% at 50% flipping to 89.35% at 70% and 92.44% at 90%.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Binary label flipping above 50%, with the paper's reversed procedure and label interpretation
source_check.reason: Text-based: Section 2.3 specifies a reversed procedure above 50%; Section 3(q3) attributes accuracy recovery to flipped label interpretation. Table 3 gives BERT-large-pool 50.86%, 89.35% and 92.44% at 50%, 70% and 90% flipping. This qualifies extension of steady degradation to this corruption and evaluation protocol.

relation.reason: Reports validation accuracy across controlled training-label corruption levels, directly testing V4's generalization component.

tranche.reason: Tests the validation-degradation component of V4 in a new setting: binary sentiment classification with training-label flipping.

source_check.notes: Table 3 reports maximum validation accuracies; learning rate and epochs were tuned for validation performance. Perfect training fit throughout the sweep is not demonstrated, and above-50% recovery uses reversed label interpretation rather than an independent-random-label endpoint.
